September 2010 # Oscillating between exuberance and fear - The seasonal downturn in copper consumption in Q3 has been less apparent than usual, given the momentum of the recovery in industrial activity and some restocking of both cathode and semis. This demand picture is detached from the erratic sentiment about global economic prospects, which has been driving LME prices. - Copper supply continues to be tight, with semis producers drawing material from exchange stocks. However, over the past month spot demand is reported to have softened and cathode premiums in China and the US have eased in August compared to July and the pace of decline in exchange stocks has flattened out. - After pushing through $7,500/t, LME prices corrected towards $7,000/t on 25th August. We expect prices to continue to be directed by macroeconomic sentiment and the trend in the value of the US dollar. The next support level is $6,900/t, but we believe that prices will hold above $7,000/t. |The supply/deman

r 3-month material on 4th August. This high point was quickly followed by a correction, as concerns over the sustainability of the US recovery saw a flight to safety by investors. The shift in sentiment led to the value of the US dollar rising sharply and saw copper prices sliding back below $7,200/t. The market then saw prices spike close to $7,500/t on 19th August, aided by the robust economic growth reported in Germany for Q2. However, lingering doubts about the strength of the US recovery, abetted by fears that inflation in China may prompt a tightening of monetary policy in the autumn, saw copper prices just as quickly retrace towards $7,000/t on 25th August. The swings in market sentiment and prices do not reflect the demand picture, however, with global consumption up by an estimated 5% y-o-y in Q3 and exchange stocks continuing to be drawn down. ### **Recovery on track in Europe and North America…** The surprisingly strong German GDP growth in Q2 (up by 3.7% y-o-y) demonstrates forcefully that the lower value of the euro has been a net positive for European economic growth. A major reason for the strong result was the 8.2% q-o-q increase in exports, led by exports to China that are up by over 30% y-o-y. The cheaper euro and the boost to exports is also benefiting France and other larger northern and central European countries. However, the uncertainties over the future of crisis-hit southern European countries and Ireland mean that these markets have not benefited as much as their northern and central European neighbours. The upturn in exports and domestic economic demand (particularly in Germany) is translating into higher than expected semis production growth. The rod, bar & sections and tube markets are covered in detail in our expanded Consumption Trends section on pages 9-10, which incorporates data formerly provided in our Copper and Copper Alloy Products monitor. The combined output of these product types rose by 26% in Western Europe as a whole in Q2. Growth was led by Italy (up by 50% y-o-y) and Germany (up by 46% y- o-y). Wirerod production in Western Europe as a whole was also up in Q2, but only by 3% y-o-y as it had declined by less than other product types during the downturn in 2008-2009. On a sector basis in Europe, demand from the moribund construction sector continues to lag that from other end-use sectors, with domestic appliances, electrical and mechanical engineering and automotive markets leading t

he increases. 

The recovery in copper demand in Europe has resulted in generally shorter holiday shutdowns of manufacturing production, including at copper semis plants.  However, sustained consumption levels have not been enough to boost spot premiums, which remain flat at the $90-100/t level. 

In the USA, demand prospects had looked quite solid in the Spring, but since then sentiment has been undermined by fears over the sustainability of the economic recovery and the possibility of a double-dip. The collapse in existing home sales in July by over 25% y-o-y to a 15 year low shows just how far the

housing market has to go to clear the imbalances in the market that were built up over the boom years.  This will continue to pose a threat to economic growth and copper consumption from the construction sector, with a further decline in house prices acting as a drag on efforts to repair household and financial sector balance sheets.  That said, we see no serious signs of copper semis growth being impacted by the macroeconomic uncertainty.  We estimate that total semis production increased by around 10% y-o-y in Q2 and will grow at a similar rate in Q3.  Growth is being sustained by the momentum built up by the bounce in industrial activity across most sectors from last year’s trough.  As in Europe, there is less of a seasonal slowdown in demand in North America, although spot demand is reported to be soft at the moment and as a result, cathode premiums have drifted lower by 0.5¢/lb to 5.0-6.5¢/lb over the past month. 

### **…with China and rest of Asia still looking solid…** 

Chinese semis production growth in Q3 is also more robust than is usually the case, with many of the larger tube producers reporting that they may not see any slowdown at all this year due to the hot weather in northern China boosting air conditioner tube demand.  Wirerod mills are also looking forward to good demand in September, as demand for wire and cable is on course for growth of more than 10% in 2010, led by low voltage energy cable and winding wire.  However, there is not unalloyed optimism, with evidence of the usual seasonal slowdown in demand at plate, sheet and strip producers and they do not expect a pick up until October.  This has resulted in premia for imported cathode slipping back to a $70-120/t range over the past month. 

In Japan, the dichotomy between the weak macro view and strong copper demand is particularly striking. GDP growth slowed in Q2 to 2.7% y-o-y from 4.3% in Q1, with overall industrial production growth down even more markedly, from a 7% q-o-q increase in Q1 to only 1.4% in Q2.  At the same time though, wire and cable shipments in July were reported to have risen by 2.9% y-o-y, the 8th straight month of increases. With bare wire sales up by 11.3%, total copper wire and cable shipments rose by 5.6% y-o-y.  This shows the buo

yancy of copper demand relative to the broader economy, which in part is derived from exports but also domestic appliance, electronics and automotive demand. However, the rise in the value of the yen is likely to lead to a dampening of exports of copper and copper containing products over the balance of the year. ### **…drawing down exchange stocks further…** Given that demand continues to outstrip expectations, despite the weakening of the macro outlook, exchange stocks have remained on a downward trend over the past month. Consumers and merchants entered the year in an extremely cautious mood and booked the minimal level of cathode on contract. As we have highlighted above, demand this year has been generally stronger than expected, which we believe has led to marginal restocking of both cathode and semis throughout the supply chain. Despite the stronger demand we have seen the decline in LME stocks begin to flatten out over the past month. However, cancelled warrants remain at a relatively high 7% of total stocks, which we attribute in part to the just-in-time nature of stock management. Some consumers find it more convenient to take material out of exchange warehouses rather than committing to contracted deliveries from producers, for example. Therefore, we are likely to see a continued “churning” of exchange stocks over the next few months. ### **…as production growth slackens** The drawdown in stocks is supported by an anticpated q-on-q decline in refined production in Q3. In part this is due to planned smelter maintenance closures in July and August, most of which are in China, where reported refined production in July fell by 5.7% m-o-m but was still up by 16% y-o-y. Chinese smelters will face difficulty in maintaining y-o-y growth rates at these high double digit levels, as it will be a challenge to secure a growing share of global raw material requirements. In fact, we believe that the spate of delays to smelter expansions this year and beyond is in part due to the lack of available feed. As for the announcement that some Chinese smelters are marked for closure due to failure to meet environmental regulations amounts to less than meets the eye. Only 145,000t/y of coppe

r capacity was identified and most of these are being replaced by new larger smelters. For more details on this announcement and its implications see the Copper China Fortnightly (email of 13 August and downloadable from the website). The majority of the second quarter’s results are now in and we estimate that mine output in Q2 fell y-o-y by 1.2%. Refined output had risen by an estimated 7.4% y-o-y in Q2 but is set to fall in Q3, by 1.4% y-o-y due to a combination of lower mine production, the planned smelter maintenance closures and the permanent closures of the Flin Flon and Kidd Creek smelters in Canada. In addition, scrap availability remains constrained, although relatively more material became available in the US and Europe, leading to wider discounts in August. In China, the usual scrap trader behaviour is in evidence, with material being held back in the hope that LME prices will continue to rise after breaching $7,000/t. ### **Price under pressure, but not exceptionally so** For the moment, we see the price continuing to be driven by macroeconomic sentiment and movement in the value of the US dollar rather than the immediate market fundamentals. With the dollar likely to continue to strengthen in the short term, and barring any sustained positive economic news over the next Fund investment only caught up month, we expect prices could test downside support with the price in Feb 2010 Apr 2008-Aug 2010 of $6,900/t. Data: CRU,WBMS|||||**_._**||||||**.**|||| © 2010 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 8 of 16 September 2010 Copper Monitor www.crumonitor.com # Consumption trends ## **Copper tube production up 12.6% q-o-q in Q2** We estimate that global copper tube production in the second quarter of 2010 was 618,000t, up 12.6% q- o-q and 5.3% y-o-y. This was the third sequential upturn in output since Q4 2009, which has been mainly supported by robust production in Developing Asia and North East Asia. The world copper tube market has improved as well, with total offtake of 620,000t in Q2 2010, compared to 547,000t in the previous quarter. Trade data shows that world export volume in the second quarter was almost back to the precrisis level in Q3 2008. More specifically, exports from China, South Korea, the US and Germany have outperformed our expectations in Q2, indicating a real recovery in the global market. On a regional basis, both Europe and Asia saw y-o-y growth in copper tube consumption for the first half of this year, while North America was still below year-ago levels. Copper tube offtake in the US was 87,000t in Q2 2010, compared to 115,000t for the same period in 2009. Housing starts were up 1.7% from June to July 2010, but were 7% down on July 2009 level. Industry participants said that funds from the government stimulus package for the construction industry are being spent more slowly than many had expected, according to the Associated General Contractors of America. US-based copper tube producer **Wolverine Tube** reported an unaudited net loss of US$5.9M for Q2 2010, compared to a net loss of US$11.1M in Q2 2009. The company has incurred net losses since 2005, which were a result of restructuring activities and interest expense. Orders and shipments have begun to recover in Q2 2010 but it is still expecting to report operating losses in 2010, depending on copper prices and the consistency in the economic recovery. The anti-dumping case should also support tube production in the US. Copper tube production in Western Europe edged up 2.9% y-o-y in the first half of this year, with Germany being the main driver of the momentum. German output was 72,000t in H1 2010, up 27.4% compared to the same period of 2009. **KME** said that consumption from the appliance sector, especially in Germany, has grown and demand for pipes used in refrigeration and air conditioning

was robust. **Wieland** reported that the market for its products has recovered significantly.  The company has decided to increase the fabrication prices by 5% as of 1<sup>st</sup> September 2010 in order to counter rising costs.  Italian and French tube consumption increased y-o-y by 13.8% and 18.3%, respectively, in H1 2010.  In Spain, the UK and Greece, Q2 consumption was still below the 2009 figures due to the ongoing construction downturn. We expect that Western European tube demand will stay at a reasonable level for the second half of this year, but output volumes will depend on the speed of the recovery. 

Japan and Korea, saw production increase by 13.9% and 13.1% in the first half of this year.  The joint output of China and Other Asia also increased by 9.2% y-o-y in H1 2010.  20 leading Chinese copper tube manufacturers were operating at an average rate of 74.2% (lower than the June figure) due to the traditional weak season in China, according to Antaike.  Some producers are worried about the effect from strict policies in the real estate market.  Nevertheless, **Hailiang Anhui Copper** went ahead with its plans to construct a 48,000t copper tube project in July, which will be commissioned in April 2011.  In India, **Nissan Copper** announced in late-August that its facility in Shanvel, Silvassa, will start trial partial production of copper tubes for air conditioning, refrigeration and plumbing applications in the next 15 days, presumably in September.  The ROW region saw production fall by 4.4% y-o-y in H1 2010.   In August, **Abu Dhabi Basic Industries Corporation** has invited companies to bid by the end of September to build a US$50M copper tube plant at Taweelah.  The new 30,000-40,000t/y tube mill is to feed demand in the MENA region as new construction projects require copper tube for air conditioning and water systems.  The whole region currently imports tube from Turkey, Ukraine and Asia.

## **Restocking and industrial demand drives alloy rod consumption** 

World production of alloy rods, bars and sections increased by 30.6% in the first half of 2010, given that all regional volumes are now above year-ago levels. The y-o-y growth was mainly attributed to higher volumes in Developing and North East Asia, particularly in Japan and China.  Europe also experienced a 32.3% increase in alloy rod production in H1 2010, as output grew from 199,000t in Q2 2009 to 279,000t in Q2 2010.  Market participants said that consumers are restocking and placing more orders now as opposed to destocking the same time last year, given the development of a recovery in the global economy.  We believe that the y-o-y upward trend will continue in the second half of this year but possibly at a slower pace, as it will be compared against higher volumes in H2 2009. 

In Western Europe, Germany and Italy were the best performers for H1

2010, with output growing y-o-y by 44.8% and 44.7%, respectively.  This is supported by robust demand from the domestic automotive and mechanical sectors, and also by improved orders from their export markets.  French exports were 15,000t in Q2 2010, much higher than 6,200t in Q2 2009.  German exports were up 55.6% y-o-y to 29,100t in Q1 2010 and we estimate this to be around 28,400t in Q2 2010. **KME** reported in August that its total semis output for H1 2010 was up 21% y-o-y to 264,000t as industrial demand recovered well. **Swissmetal** said that new orders for its products jumped 59% y-o-y in H1 2010 due to greatly increased demand, which ensured good capacity utilisation.  The company remains optimistic for the second half of the year and it has launched programs in the production area to improve cost and organisational structure. Regional consumption increased from 158,000t in Q2 2009 to 216,000t in Q2 2010. 

Moving onto Asia, the Japanese alloy rod market showed an expansion of 74.2% y-o-y to 97,000t in H1 2010.  This was partly due to consumer restocking activity, and also a surge in downstream demand. **Kitz Metal Works** , the largest Japanese brass bar manufacturer said that it has increased production by 500t/m to 3,500t/m since July as it cannot meet recovering demand from the automotive and appliance sectors as it closed a subsidiary in September 2009.  The company has increased its workforce by 10% and the shift at the casting line at the start of 2010.  Meanwhile, **Nippon Shindo Co Ltd** has begun test runs of melting and casting at its new factory completed recently and shipments are expected to start in January 2011.  The Asian market grew 31.9% y-o-y to 796,000t in the H1 2010 and we believe it will continue to drive the momentum of global consumption in H2 2010. 

## **Leading wire and cable company results** 

**Nexans** reported a net upturn in sales (in organic terms) in the second quarter, up 12% from Q1. Sales in H1 were €2.1B at constant metal prices, up from €2.085B a year earlier, but this was down 5.3% y-o-y in organic terms.  Nexans’ Energy business has announced its intention to close the Latina plant in Italy (mainly serving the Italian power distribution cable market) and the Lorena facility in Brazil. **Prysmian** on reported the first signs of recovery in demand across all businesses (even construction related) after several negative quarters, with an organic sales growth of 4.3% in Q2 2010, mitigating the 11.2% decline seen in Q1.  H1 2010 sales were €2.15B, up from €1.85B in H1 2009 but an organic decline of 3.4%. The order book for HV and submarine projects rose to €1.4B as of July, so year-end profit targets are confirmed. **Draka** published its H1 2010 sales figures and commented that the company saw signs of cautious recovery in several cable market segments. # Industry News ## **Mine Production** - Unionised workers at **Batu Hijau** mine started a strike on 2nd August demanding overtime fee payment. On 6th August it was announced that the strike had ended after management and the unions agreed to further talks on the subject of overtime payment. The mine is partially owned and operated by a subsidiary of **Newmont Mining** , and Newmont have announced that production will not be affected. In 2010, Batu Hijau is expected to produce 275,000t of copper-in-concentrate. - The management of **Collahuasi** (Chile) has presented a proposal to the unionised workers aiming to start early negotiations for the renewal of labour contracts that are due to expire in October. According to various media reports the unions have not accepted the proposal, and management may be facing a period of tough negotiations in the wake of mass protests by subcontractor workers in May, which were supported by the full-time employees’ unions.
